Verify actual WordPress record IDs and source freshness before reporting completed work.

arguments.title: How to describe a recurring flat tire before your workshop visit
arguments.excerpt: A tire that keeps going soft is easier to diagnose when you can say when the air disappears and what you were riding on. Here is what to notice before you bring the bike in.
arguments.summary: New blog draft: visit-preparation guide for recurring flat tires, linked to the puncture repair service page.
arguments.reasoning: Distinct reader task from post 100 (service statement) and post 200 (tire size markings). Built only on stored site evidence; no prices, hours, credentials or testimonials invented.
arguments.content:
A tire that goes soft once is usually a simple puncture. A tire that keeps going soft is a pattern, and patterns are much easier to trace when someone can tell us what the pattern looks like. Our workshop repairs bicycle tire punctures and inspects tires, and we ask customers to describe when air loss occurs. This post explains what to notice so that description is useful.

Notice when the air disappears

Timing is the single most helpful detail. Before your visit, try to place your flat in one of these rough groups:

  • The tire goes flat within minutes of pumping it up.
  • It holds air for a few hours, then sags.
  • It holds for several days or a week and slowly softens.
  • It only goes down while you are riding, not while the bike is parked.

A fast loss and a slow weekly loss point in different directions, so saying which one you have saves guesswork at the bench.

Note where and how you were riding

Air loss that starts after a specific ride is worth mentioning. Useful things to recall include the surface you were on, whether you hit a kerb or pothole, whether you were carrying extra load such as bags or a child seat, and whether the flat happened in cold or wet weather. If the tire failed at a predictable spot on your usual route, say so.

Check the pressure habit, not just the tire

Think about how you normally inflate the tire. Do you use a floor pump with a gauge, a hand pump, or a garage air line? Do you top the tire up weekly, monthly, or only when it feels soft? Riding at low pressure can cause repeat flats, so your inflation routine is part of the story rather than a side detail.

Remember any recent work on the wheel

Tell us if anything changed on that wheel recently. A new tire, a new inner tube, a patched tube, a swapped wheel, or a fix done at the roadside all change what we look for first. If you patched it yourself and the patch held for a while before failing, that is a useful clue too.

Bring the evidence with you

If you removed the tube, bring it along instead of throwing it out. The position and shape of the hole tells us a lot. Bring the bike with the wheel still fitted where you can, and if anything is still stuck in the tread, leave it in place rather than pulling it out, so we can see where it entered.

A short description you can reuse

You do not need technical language. A sentence in this shape covers most of what we need: "The rear tire holds air for about two days, it started after a wet ride on a gravel path last month, I pump it with a floor pump roughly every two weeks, and the tube was patched once since then."

What happens next

When you arrive, we inspect the tire and the tube and work through the causes your description makes most likely. You can read more about the service itself on our bicycle puncture repair page. If you are unsure which tire you are dealing with when you call, our post on reading tire size markings explains where to find the numbers printed on the sidewall.
